entries.name: Vitamin A
entries.note: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin found in foods like dairy, fish, and orange and leafy green vegetables. Too much preformed vitamin A can be harmful, especially during pregnancy, so talk with your clinician before taking more than your label says.

entries.name: Vitamin C
entries.note: Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble vitamin found in many fruits and vegetables. Supplements come in a few forms, and your label says which one you have.

entries.name: Vitamin D
entries.note: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin, and some fat in the same meal helps the body absorb it. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Vitamin E
entries.note: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin found in nuts, seeds, and vegetable oils. In supplement form it can raise bleeding risk for people on blood thinners such as warfarin, so check with your clinician if you take one.

entries.name: Vitamin K
entries.note: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin found in leafy greens and some fermented foods. It can interact seriously with the blood thinner warfarin, so talk with your clinician before starting or stopping it if you take one.

entries.name: Thiamin (Vitamin B1)
entries.note: Thiamin is a B vitamin found in whole grains, pork, fish, beans, and fortified foods. It's often part of B-complex and multivitamin products.

entries.name: Riboflavin (Vitamin B2)
entries.note: Riboflavin is a B vitamin found in eggs, dairy, meat, mushrooms, and fortified grains. It's often part of B-complex and multivitamin products.

entries.name: Niacin (Vitamin B3)
entries.note: Niacin is a B vitamin found in poultry, fish, grains, and many other foods. Supplements come in different forms, such as nicotinic acid and niacinamide, so check your label for which one you have.

entries.name: Pantothenic Acid (Vitamin B5)
entries.note: Pantothenic acid is a B vitamin found in almost all foods. It's often part of B-complex and multivitamin products.

entries.name: Vitamin B6
entries.note: Vitamin B6 is a water-soluble vitamin found in many foods. Taking high amounts from supplements for a long time can cause nerve damage, so talk with your clinician before taking more than your label says.

entries.name: Biotin (Vitamin B7)
entries.note: Biotin is a B vitamin found in foods like eggs, fish, meat, seeds, and nuts. Biotin supplements can cause false results on some lab tests, so tell your clinician you take it before blood work.

entries.name: Folate (Folic Acid)
entries.note: Folate is a B vitamin found naturally in leafy greens, beans, and fruit. Folic acid is the form used in most supplements and fortified foods.

entries.name: Vitamin B12
entries.note: Vitamin B12 is found naturally in animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs, and dairy. Plant foods only have it when fortified, as some cereals and nutritional yeasts are.

entries.name: B-Complex
entries.note: B-complex products combine several B vitamins in one pill. Amounts vary a lot between products, so your label is the best guide for yours.

entries.name: Multivitamin
entries.note: Multivitamins combine several vitamins and minerals, and the mix varies widely between products. They can't take the place of a varied diet, and your label has the directions for your product.

entries.name: Prenatal Vitamin
entries.note: Prenatal vitamins are multivitamins designed for pregnancy. Your clinician or pharmacist can help you choose one and check it against anything else you take.

entries.name: Vitamin D3 + K2
entries.note: These products pair vitamin D3 with vitamin K2, both fat-soluble vitamins. Vitamin K can interact with the blood thinner warfarin, so check with your clinician first if you take one.

entries.name: Calcium
entries.note: Calcium carbonate is absorbed best with food, while calcium citrate is absorbed well with or without food. Your label says which form you have and how to take it.

entries.name: Magnesium
entries.note: Magnesium supplements come in many forms, such as glycinate, citrate, and oxide. High amounts from supplements can cause diarrhea or cramping, so follow your label.

entries.name: Iron
entries.note: Iron supplements can upset the stomach for some people, and vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from plant foods. Keep iron products out of children's reach, because an accidental overdose is dangerous for kids.

entries.name: Zinc
entries.note: Zinc is a mineral found in meat, seafood, beans, and nuts. Taking a lot of zinc for a long time can lower copper levels, so follow your label.

entries.name: Potassium
entries.note: Potassium is a mineral found in many fruits, vegetables, beans, and dairy foods. Some medicines affect potassium, so check with your clinician or pharmacist before adding a supplement.

entries.name: Selenium
entries.note: Selenium is a mineral found in seafood, meat, grains, and especially Brazil nuts. Getting too much can cause problems like garlic breath and brittle nails, so follow your label.

entries.name: Iodine
entries.note: Iodine is a mineral the body uses to make thyroid hormones. It's found in seafood, dairy, and iodized salt.

entries.name: Chromium
entries.note: Chromium is a mineral found in small amounts in many foods, including meat, whole grains, and some fruits and vegetables. It's included in many multivitamins as well as on its own.

entries.name: Copper
entries.note: Copper is a mineral found in shellfish, nuts, seeds, and whole grains. High amounts of zinc from supplements can make it harder for the body to absorb copper.

entries.name: Manganese
entries.note: Manganese is a mineral found in whole grains, nuts, leafy vegetables, and tea. It's most often found in multivitamins rather than on its own.

entries.name: Choline
entries.note: Choline is a nutrient found in many foods, including eggs, meat, fish, and beans. Supplements come in several forms, so check your label for which one you have.

entries.name: Electrolytes
entries.note: Electrolyte products usually contain sodium and potassium, and sometimes magnesium or calcium. Amounts vary a lot between products, so check the label, especially if you're watching your salt.

entries.name: Omega-3 (Fish Oil)
entries.note: Omega-3 supplements include fish oil, krill oil, cod liver oil, and algal oil. Side effects are usually mild, like an unpleasant taste or heartburn, and your label has the directions for your product.

entries.name: Creatine
entries.note: Creatine is a compound stored in muscles, and the body makes some on its own. It usually causes a little weight gain because muscles hold more water.

entries.name: Protein Powder
entries.note: Most protein powders contain whey, a protein from milk, while others use plant sources like pea or soy. Your label lists the protein per scoop and the other ingredients.

entries.name: Collagen
entries.note: Collagen is a protein, and collagen supplements are made from animal sources such as cattle or fish. Your label lists the source and the amount per serving.

entries.name: Beta-Alanine
entries.note: Beta-alanine is an amino acid found in meat, poultry, and fish. Larger amounts can cause a tingling or prickling feeling in the skin, so follow your label.

entries.name: BCAAs
entries.note: BCAAs are three amino acids: leucine, isoleucine, and valine. They're found naturally in protein foods like meat, fish, and milk.

entries.name: Glutamine
entries.note: Glutamine is an amino acid the body makes on its own and also gets from food. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: L-Carnitine
entries.note: Carnitine is a nutrient found in many foods, especially meat, and the body makes enough for most people. Supplements come in a few forms, such as L-carnitine and acetyl-L-carnitine.

entries.name: L-Theanine
entries.note: L-theanine is an amino acid found naturally in tea leaves. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Caffeine
entries.note: Caffeine shows up in coffee, tea, energy drinks, and many workout products. Amounts vary a lot, so check labels to know your total for the day.

entries.name: Probiotic
entries.note: Probiotics are live microorganisms, and products differ in which strains they contain. Some need refrigeration while others don't, so check your label for storage and the use-by date.

entries.name: Fiber (Psyllium)
entries.note: Fiber supplements like psyllium are taken with plenty of liquid. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Melatonin
entries.note: Melatonin is a hormone the body makes, and supplements are usually taken in the evening. Studies have found that the amount in many products, including gummies, doesn't match the label.

entries.name: Ashwagandha
entries.note: Ashwagandha is an herb from Ayurvedic tradition. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported, and it should be avoided during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

entries.name: Turmeric (Curcumin)
entries.note: Turmeric is a spice, and curcumin is one of its main compounds. Some highly absorbable curcumin products may harm the liver, so check with your clinician if you have liver concerns.

entries.name: CoQ10
entries.note: CoQ10 is a compound the body makes on its own. It may interact with the blood thinner warfarin and with insulin, so check with your clinician if you take either.

entries.name: Glucosamine
entries.note: Glucosamine is often sold together with chondroitin. The pair has been linked to a higher risk of bleeding in people taking warfarin, so check with your clinician if you take a blood thinner.

entries.name: Chondroitin
entries.note: Chondroitin is often sold together with glucosamine. The pair has been linked to a higher risk of bleeding in people taking warfarin, so check with your clinician if you take a blood thinner.

entries.name: Elderberry
entries.note: Elderberry products are made from cooked or processed berries. Raw or unripe elderberries and other parts of the plant contain substances that can make people sick.

entries.name: Echinacea
entries.note: Echinacea is a plant related to daisies, sunflowers, and ragweed. Products vary in which species and plant parts they use, so your label is the best guide for yours.

entries.name: Ginseng
entries.note: Ginseng is a root used in traditional Chinese medicine, and products include Asian (Panax) and American ginseng. Your label says which kind you have.

entries.name: Green Tea Extract
entries.note: Green tea extracts come as tablets and capsules. Although uncommon, liver injury has been reported with these products, so check with your clinician if you have liver concerns.

entries.name: St. John's Wort
entries.note: St. John's wort interacts with many medicines, sometimes in serious ways. Check with your pharmacist or clinician before taking it alongside any medicine.

entries.name: Valerian
entries.note: Valerian supplements are made from the roots of the valerian plant. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Garlic
entries.note: Garlic supplements may raise the risk of bleeding. Check with your clinician if you take a blood thinner or aspirin, or before surgery.

entries.name: Ginger
entries.note: Ginger is a plant whose root is used as a spice and in supplements. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Ginkgo
entries.note: Ginkgo supplements come from the leaves of the ginkgo tree. It may raise bleeding risk in people taking blood thinners such as warfarin, so check with your clinician first.

entries.name: Saw Palmetto
entries.note: Saw palmetto comes from a small palm tree, also called the American dwarf palm. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Lutein & Zeaxanthin
entries.note: Lutein and zeaxanthin are carotenoids, a group of plant pigments. They're part of the AREDS2 eye vitamin formula studied by the National Eye Institute.

entries.name: Rhodiola
entries.note: Rhodiola is a plant that grows in cold regions and at high altitudes. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Milk Thistle
entries.note: Silymarin is the main group of compounds in milk thistle extract. Some products have been found to contain amounts that differ from the label.

entries.name: Cranberry
entries.note: Cranberry supplements are made from the fruit, often as a dried extract. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Flaxseed
entries.note: Flaxseed and flaxseed oil come from the seeds of the flax plant and contain ALA, a plant omega-3. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Chamomile
entries.note: Chamomile is a daisy-like plant often used as a tea. People allergic to related plants, such as ragweed or daisies, are more likely to react to it.

entries.name: Black Cohosh
entries.note: Black cohosh supplements are made from the roots of a North American plant. Cases of liver damage have been reported, so check with your clinician if you have liver concerns.

entries.name: Evening Primrose Oil
entries.note: Evening primrose oil comes from the plant's seeds and contains omega-6 fatty acids, including GLA. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.

entries.name: Cinnamon
entries.note: Cinnamon supplements are made from the dried bark of a few related trees, including Ceylon and cassia cinnamon. Your label has the amount and directions for your product.
